title: How to Price a Service Call Without Losing Money
description: You quoted $150 for a service call—but after drive time, parts, and two hours on site, did you actually make money? In this practical JobMargin tutorial, we'll price a service call by accounting for trip fees, labor, parts markup, and overhead. We'll also compare markup and margin so every quote protects your profit. Try JobMargin free for 7 days: https://job-margin.com

scenes.narration: You quoted one hundred fifty dollars for a service call. But after drive time, parts, and two hours on site... did you actually make money? In this video, we'll build a service call price that pays you for the whole job—not just the time your tools are in your hand.

Open JobMargin's service call pricing calculator at job-margin dot com slash tools slash service-call-pricing. Start with the basics: the trip fee, the time you expect to spend on site, and your hourly rate. The calculator turns those inputs into a customer price and an estimated real profit, so you can see the difference between revenue and what you keep.

First, enter your trip fee. This should cover the cost of getting to the customer: fuel, vehicle wear, and the time spent driving. A trip fee is not an extra charge to apologize for. It is part of the work. If a round trip takes forty-five minutes, that is time your business is spending on this customer, even before you arrive. Try a sixty-five dollar trip fee, then change it to twenty-five and watch the projected profit move.

Next, enter the on-site hours and your target hourly rate. Say the repair takes two hours at ninety dollars per hour. That creates one hundred eighty dollars of labor revenue. But your hourly rate is not the same as your take-home pay. It has to carry your non-billable time, insurance, software, tools, and the profit you need to stay in business. Add drive time mentally as well: a two-hour repair can consume nearly three hours of your day.

Now add parts and materials. Enter your actual cost, not the price you hope to pay. Then use the parts markup field to cover purchasing time, stock that goes unused, warranty risk, and handling. For example, a fifty dollar part with a forty percent markup is billed at seventy dollars. The calculator shows the customer total and the contribution from materials separately, making it easier to spot a quote that looks good but leaves no room for mistakes.

The final lever is overhead. Overhead is the cost of being ready to work: licenses, accounting, phone service, rent, vehicle payments, and marketing. Set a percentage that reflects your business instead of leaving it at zero. With a sixty-five dollar trip fee, one hundred eighty dollars of labor, seventy dollars billed for parts, and overhead included, compare the total price with the real profit. Change one input at a time. This is how you find the price floor below which the job is not worth taking.

One pricing detail trips up many contractors: markup and margin are not interchangeable. A forty percent markup on one hundred dollars costs forty dollars and bills one hundred forty. But the margin is forty divided by one hundred forty—about twenty-nine percent. Open JobMargin's markup versus margin converter at job-margin dot com slash tools slash markup-margin-converter. Enter your cost and target markup, then use the result when you build a quote. Small percentage mistakes become big dollars across a full calendar.

Before you send the quote, run the whole job through the calculator one more time. Ask: does the trip fee pay for the route, does labor pay for the entire block of time, are parts protected by a sensible markup, and is overhead included?
